title: Fitting cabinet knobs and cup pulls
subtitle: Mark and drill consistent fixing positions for knobs and cup pulls on kitchen or furniture cabinet doors and drawer fronts
excerpt: How to fit cabinet knobs and cup pulls to kitchen doors and drawer fronts. Covers marking a consistent position on every door and drawer, drilling clean through-holes, and fitting the hardware with machine screws.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK architectural ironmongery trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A recessed drawer handle in which the finger slides into a shallow cup to pull the drawer. Fitted flush or slightly recessed into the drawer front. Traditionally used on Shaker-style and simple furniture. Fixed with a single machine screw from the back of the drawer front.

content.text: Fitting handles is the last step in a kitchen or furniture project, and inconsistent positioning shows immediately. The job is to use a simple card template to mark every door and drawer at the same point, drill cleanly, and fix. A
or knob takes one through-hole; a bar handle takes two.

Cut a card template with the handle position marked as a hole in the card. Standard position for a door knob: 50 mm in from the edge, 100 mm from the top or bottom edge on a door; on a drawer front, centred on the width and height. Mark the centre of the template clearly. Align the card to the corner of each door and drawer to mark the hole position consistently. Using the same template for every piece prevents the drift that comes from measuring each one individually.

Drill from the front face. Use masking tape on the back face to prevent the drill bit blowing out the surface as it exits. The hole diameter should match the machine screw thread: typically a 4 mm bit for an M4 screw. For a bar handle with two fixing points, mark both holes using the template simultaneously. Check the distance between holes matches the handle bore centres (typically 96 mm or 128 mm for standard handles) before drilling.

Thread the machine screw through the knob or pull, then through the door from the back. Tighten with a screwdriver. For a knob, a single screw from the back goes through the door and into the threaded shank of the knob. Do not overtighten; MDF and veneered board strip easily. For a cup pull set into the face of a drawer, the screw passes through the board into the threaded cup body from the back.

Once all handles are fitted, close all doors and stand back. Any handle that is higher or lower than the run is visible immediately. Check the template position against the offending door and re-drill if necessary; slightly enlarged holes can be back-filled with a solid wood filler and re-drilled once set.

attrs.symptom: Machine screw spins without tightening the knob
attrs.cause: The screw thread has stripped in the knob's threaded shank, or the shank is too short for the door thickness.
attrs.fix: Use a longer machine screw to engage fresh thread. If the shank is stripped, the knob must be replaced.

attrs.symptom: The drill bit blows out a large chip on the back face of the door
attrs.cause: Drilling too fast without backing the work or using masking tape.
attrs.fix: Fill the blowout with a fine surface filler, sand flat when dry, and touch up the paint. Drill future holes with masking tape on the back face and slow the drill speed as the bit breaks through.
